sections.title: A verb said twice
sections.content: You know the present subjunctive from A2 Unit 27 and the concessive connectors of this unit. There is a short way to say "it makes no difference what, who, where or how": repeat the verb in the subjunctive around a relative word. *Pase lo que pase* means "whatever happens". Spanish has no single word for "whatever" here, so it says "may happen what may happen". The rest of the sentence is what stays true: *Pase lo que pase, te voy a apoyar*.

sections.title: The pattern
rows: One way or another, however it has to be done
Whether you like it or not

sections.title: How it works
sections.content: The formula has three parts: a verb in the present subjunctive, a relative word (*lo que*, *quien*, *donde*, *como*), and the same verb again. The two verbs always have the same person and tense, because the speaker is talking about one subject: *diga lo que diga*, *digas lo que digas*. The clause can come first, followed by a comma, or last without one: *Voy a terminar este trabajo sea como sea*. A second kind uses *o no* in place of a relative word: *Quieras o no, tienes que ir*.

items.spanish: Pase lo que pase, te voy a apoyar.
items.english: Whatever happens, I'm going to support you.

items.spanish: Diga lo que diga, no voy a cambiar de opinión.
items.english: Whatever he says, I'm not going to change my mind.

items.spanish: Voy a terminar este trabajo sea como sea.
items.english: I'm going to finish this work one way or another.

items.spanish: Estés donde estés, llámame el domingo.
items.english: Wherever you are, call me on Sunday.

sections.content: Both verbs must be in the subjunctive and must match: *pase lo que pase*, never *pase lo que pasa*. Do not confuse the formula with a question: *¿Qué pasa?* asks "what is happening?", while *pase lo que pase* says that nothing will change your decision.
